title: Column Transformer
abstract:
Real datasets are heterogeneous: numerical columns need scaling and imputation,
categorical columns need encoding, and some columns need to be dropped
altogether. ColumnTransformer applies different transformations to
different columns inside a single object and combines all the transformed
output into one matrix. This document covers the API, column selection by name
and by dtype, the remainder parameter, nesting pipelines inside branches,
recovering feature names after transformation, and the ordering guarantees that
make the output reproducible.

blocks.t: The Problem It Solves
From the notes

In scikit-learn, ColumnTransformer applies different transformations to
different columns in a single pipeline. In real data:

items: Some columns — need to be dropped

blocks.t:
ColumnTransformer solves this. It combines all transformed output into
one single matrix.

blocks.cap:
One object takes a heterogeneous dataframe, routes each group of
 columns to its own transformer, and horizontally stacks the results into a
 single numeric matrix ready for a model.

blocks.t: What it replaces

Without it, you write something like this — and then write it again, correctly,
for production:

# The manual version. Every line is a chance to make a mistake.
num = ["age", "income"]; cat = ["city", "plan"]

imp    = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit(X_tr[num])
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(imp.transform(X_tr[num]))
enc    = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore").fit(X_tr[cat])

X_tr_num = scaler.transform(imp.transform(X_tr[num]))
X_tr_cat = enc.transform(X_tr[cat]).toarray()
X_tr_out = np.hstack([X_tr_num, X_tr_cat])

X_te_num = scaler.transform(imp.transform(X_te[num]))   # must not refit
X_te_cat = enc.transform(X_te[cat]).toarray()           # must not refit
X_te_out = np.hstack([X_te_num, X_te_cat])              # must be same order

Three fitted objects to track, three chances to accidentally call fit on
test, and a column order you must keep consistent by hand. The
ColumnTransformer version is four lines and cannot get any of those
wrong.
The API
Anatomy of the constructor
ColumnTransformer([ (name, transformer, columns), \ldots ])

rows: A string you choose. Used for get_params and for grid-search keys such as "num__scale__with_mean"
Any estimator with fit/transform; or the literal string "drop" or "passthrough"
A list of names, a list of indices, a boolean mask, a callable, or a make_column_selector

blocks.t: The three special values

rows: Discard these columns entirely. This is how you handle the notes' third case — "some columns need to be dropped"
Include the columns unchanged. Useful for columns that are already binary or already scaled
What to do with columns you did not name. Default is "drop"; set "passthrough" to keep them

blocks.t: The remainder default silently drops columns

The default is remainder="drop". Any column you forget to list simply
disappears — no warning, no error, just a model trained on fewer features than
you thought. Being explicit is safer: list every column, or set
remainder="passthrough" and know that unnamed columns arrive raw
(and will break the model if they are strings).
Selecting columns by dtype instead of by name

Hard-coding column names breaks the moment the schema changes.
make_column_selector selects dynamically:

rows: all columns whose name starts with amt_

blocks.t: Ordering is guaranteed

Output columns appear in the order the transformers were declared, with
remainder last. This matters: it is why the training matrix and the
production matrix have identical column meanings, and it is what makes
get_feature_names_out() trustworthy.
Nesting: a Pipeline Inside a Branch

A numeric column usually needs two steps — impute, then scale. A
ColumnTransformer branch accepts any estimator, and a Pipeline is
an estimator, so you nest:

rows: TfidfVectorizer() (note: takes a 1-D column, so pass "col" not ["col"])

blocks.t: The 1-D vs 2-D gotcha

Most transformers expect a 2-D input, so you pass a list:
["age", "income"]. Text vectorisers (CountVectorizer,
TfidfVectorizer) expect a 1-D sequence, so you pass a bare string:
"review_text". Passing the list form to a vectoriser raises a confusing
error about the input shape.
Recovering Feature Names

After one-hot encoding, column 47 of your matrix is meaningless unless you can
name it. get_feature_names_out() reconstructs the names, prefixed by
the branch name:

num__age, num__income, cat__city_Delhi,
cat__city_Pune, cat__plan_premium, \dots

This is what lets you attach coefficients or feature importances back to real
column names — without it, model interpretation after a
ColumnTransformer is guesswork.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, make_column_selector, make_column_transformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "row_id":     np.arange(n),                              # DROP: no signal
    "age":        rng.integers(18, 70, n).astype(float),     # numeric
    "income":     rng.lognormal(10.5, .6, n),                # numeric, has NaN
    "city":       rng.choice(["mumbai","delhi","pune","kochi"], n),   # nominal
    "plan":       rng.choice(["basic","standard","premium"], n),      # ORDINAL
    "is_active":  rng.integers(0, 2, n),                     # already binary
    "review":     rng.choice(["great service","poor support",
                              "average experience"], n),     # text
})
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .10, "income"] = np.nan
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .05, "city"]   = None
y = (df.age > 40).astype(int)

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(df, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE BASIC FORM -- three column groups, three treatments
# =====================================================================
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([                       # a Pipeline INSIDE a branch
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scale",  StandardScaler()),
    ]), ["age", "income"]),

    ("nom", Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("ohe",    OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first")),
    ]), ["city"]),

    ("ord", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["basic","standard","premium"]]),
            ["plan"]),                       # ordinal -> keep the order

    ("txt", TfidfVectorizer(max_features=20), "review"),   # NOTE: bare string!

    ("keep", "passthrough", ["is_active"]),  # already binary, leave it alone

    ("junk", "drop", ["row_id"]),            # explicitly discarded
], remainder="drop")                         # anything unlisted is dropped

out = pre.fit_transform(X_tr)
print("output shape:", out.shape)
print("feature names:", pre.get_feature_names_out()[:8])
# ['num__age' 'num__income' 'nom__city_kochi' ... 'ord__plan' 'txt__great' ...]

# =====================================================================
# 2. SELECT BY DTYPE -- survives a schema change
# =====================================================================
auto = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("i", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("s", StandardScaler())]),
            make_column_selector(dtype_include=np.number)),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("i", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("o", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]),
            make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)),
])
print("auto-selected shape:", auto.fit_transform(X_tr.drop(columns="review")).shape)

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE remainder TRAP
# =====================================================================
partial = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), ["age"])])
print("default remainder='drop' keeps only:",
      partial.fit_transform(X_tr[["age", "is_active"]]).shape)   # (1500, 1)

partial_keep = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), ["age"])],
                                 remainder="passthrough")
print("remainder='passthrough' keeps:",
      partial_keep.fit_transform(X_tr[["age", "is_active"]]).shape)  # (1500, 2)
# is_active silently VANISHED in the first version. No warning was issued.

# =====================================================================
# 4. FIT ON TRAIN, TRANSFORM TEST -- one call each
# =====================================================================
X_tr_out = pre.fit_transform(X_tr)     # learns medians, categories, idf weights
X_te_out = pre.transform(X_te)         # reuses ALL of them
print("train", X_tr_out.shape, "test", X_te_out.shape)   # same width

learned = pre.named_transformers_
print("medians:", learned["num"].named_steps["impute"].statistics_.round(1))
print("cities :", learned["nom"].named_steps["ohe"].categories_)

# =====================================================================
# 5. INSIDE A PIPELINE, AND TUNED BY GRID SEARCH
# =====================================================================
full = Pipeline([("pre", pre),
                 ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("test accuracy:", full.score(X_te, y_te))

# The double-underscore path reaches INSIDE the ColumnTransformer:
#   step __ branch __ inner-step __ hyperparameter
grid = GridSearchCV(full, {
    "pre__num__impute__strategy": ["median", "mean"],
    "pre__num__scale__with_mean": [True, False],
    "clf__C":                     [0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
}, cv=3, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("best:", grid.best_params_, round(grid.best_score_, 4))

# =====================================================================
# 6. INTERPRETING THE MODEL -- names make coefficients readable
# =====================================================================
names = full.named_steps["pre"].get_feature_names_out()
coefs = full.named_steps["clf"].coef_[0]
imp = (pd.Series(coefs, index=names)
         .reindex(pd.Series(coefs, index=names).abs()
                  .sort_values(ascending=False).index))
print(imp.head(6).round(3))
# Without get_feature_names_out() this would be "column 14: 0.83" -- useless.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE SHORTHAND, when you do not need to name the branches
# =====================================================================
quick = make_column_transformer(
    (StandardScaler(),                       ["age", "income"]),
    (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["city", "plan"]),
    remainder="drop")
# Branch names are auto-generated ('standardscaler', 'onehotencoder').
# Prefer the explicit form when you intend to grid-search inside a branch.

blocks.t: Predicted output shape. $(5,\;2+2+0) = (5,\,4)$. Check after fit_transform: the shape must match this count, which is the fastest way to catch a mis-specified column list.

Order matters. The output columns follow the order of the transformers, so the first two are scaled CGPA and IQ, the next two are the city dummies (Delhi, Mumbai; Chennai is the dropped baseline). A downstream step that expects feature names must read them from get_feature_names_out(), never from its own memory.

Leakage guard. The scaler and encoder learn their statistics in fit. Fitting the whole ColumnTransformer on the training split only, then calling transform on test, keeps test statistics out of the training pipeline.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
ColumnTransformer applies different transformations to
 different columns in a single pipeline, and combines all
 transformed output into one matrix.

It exists because real data is heterogeneous: numerical columns need
 scaling/imputation, categorical columns need encoding,
 and some columns need to be dropped.

Form: (name, transformer, columns). The transformer may be
 "drop" or "passthrough".

remainder defaults to "drop" — unnamed columns vanish
 silently. Be explicit.

Branches can contain nested Pipelines, which is how a numeric
 column gets imputed then scaled.

Text vectorisers take a bare string column name (1-D); all other
 transformers take a list (2-D).

make_column_selector selects by dtype or regex, so the code
 survives schema changes.

get_feature_names_out() recovers readable names — essential
 for interpreting coefficients after one-hot encoding.
Output column order is deterministic: declaration order, remainder last.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why not just transform the columns manually with pandas?

Because you then hold several fitted objects and must reproduce the exact same
sequence, with the same fitted parameters and the same column order, in
production. ColumnTransformer makes that a single fitted object that is
serialised once and reused — which is what eliminates training/serving skew.

Q. A column disappeared from your feature matrix. What is the most likely
cause?

remainder="drop" — the default. Any column not listed in a branch is
discarded silently.

Q. How do you tune a hyperparameter of a transformer inside a
ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline?

Use the double-underscore path:
"pre__num__impute__strategy" — pipeline step, branch name, inner
step, parameter. This is why naming your branches explicitly is worth the extra
typing.

Q. You one-hot encoded and now the model's coefficients are unreadable.
Fix?

ct.get_feature_names_out() returns the reconstructed names in output
order; zip them with the coefficients. Without it you cannot map a coefficient
back to a category.
Q. Is the output column order guaranteed?

Yes — transformers appear in declaration order, with remainder last.
That determinism is what makes a serialised transformer safe to use in
production against a differently-ordered incoming dataframe, since selection is
by name.
